name: PCAL6408APWJ
title: PCAL6408A: 8-bit I2C-bus/SMBus I/O expander with level translation, interrupt, reset and Agile I/O, 1.65 V to 5.5 V
summary: The PCAL6408A adds eight general-purpose I/O lines (P0 to P7) to an I2C-bus or SMBus host at up to 400 kHz. It has two supplies: VDD(I2C-bus) sets the logic levels of SCL, SDA and RESET on the host side, and VDD(P) powers the core and the port, so the part translates between any two levels from 1.65 V to 5.5 V. Beyond the PCA6408A register set (input, output, polarity, direction) it has per-pin drive strength, input latching, 100 kΩ pull-up or pull-down resistors, interrupt masking and status, and a push-pull or open-drain port. It starts with every pin an input and every interrupt masked, and comes in TSSOP16, HVQFN16, XQFN16 and XFBGA16.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: The expander sits on a 1.8 V I2C-bus beside a master controller. Four 10 kΩ resistors pull SCL, SDA, INT and RESET up to the 1.8 V host supply, which also feeds VDD(I2C-bus). VDD(P) is a separate port supply. ADDR is tied to ground, so the address is 0100 000x. P0 reads an alarm line from another subsystem and P2 to P4 read keypad lines; P1 drives the enable of a controlled switch and P5 to P7 drive the keypad's other lines. The three keypad inputs carry optional 10 kΩ pull-ups to VDD(P), needed only on an input that can be left floating; outputs need no pull-up.

operation.text: VDD(I2C-bus) is the host's supply and sets the levels of SCL, SDA and RESET; VDD(P) powers the core and port P and sets the port's levels. Either rail can be 1.65 V to 5.5 V independently, so a 1.8 V host can run 1.8 V, 2.5 V, 3.3 V or 5 V peripherals and the reverse.

The part keeps the PCA6408A's four registers and pinout and adds drive-strength control, input latching, programmable pull resistors, interrupt mask and status registers, and a port-wide push-pull or open-drain choice. The one difference at start-up is that every interrupt is masked, so no interrupt fires during board bring-up.
The address is 0100 00, then ADDR, then R/W. ADDR is strapped HIGH or LOW, so two devices can share one bus. A 1 in the last bit selects a read and a 0 a write.

After the address is acknowledged the master sends a command byte, held in a write-only pointer register, that picks the register to access. Bits 1:0 choose among input, output, polarity and configuration; bit 6 together with bits 3:0 reaches the Agile I/O registers at 40h to 4Fh.
Reading it returns the logic level on every pin, whether the pin is an input or an output. Writes are ignored.
Sets the level driven on pins configured as outputs; it has no effect on inputs. A read returns what was written, not the pin level.
A 1 inverts the sense of that input pin in the input register; a 0 leaves it as is.
A 1 makes the pin a high-impedance input (the default), a 0 makes it an output.

Each pin has a two-bit field: 00b gives a quarter of full drive, 01b a half, 10b three quarters and 11b full drive (the default). The field sets how many of the four parallel transistor pairs in the output stage are switched in. Weaker drive slows the edges and lowers the peak switching current that flows through the supply and ground package inductance, which reduces simultaneous switching noise without extra parts.

Applies to inputs only. With the bit at 0, a change on the pin raises an interrupt, and the interrupt clears either when the input register is read or when the pin returns to its old state before that read. With the bit at 1, the new level is captured in the input register and stays there, with the interrupt, until the register is read, even if the pin goes back; the next read then shows the live level. If a latched and an unlatched input change together and the unlatched one returns, the interrupt stays and a read shows only the latched change and clears the interrupt. Changing a pin from latched to unlatched does not clear a pending interrupt.

A 1 in 43h connects the pin's resistor; 44h then picks pull-up (1, the default) or pull-down (0). The resistor is 100 kΩ typ, 50 kΩ min, 150 kΩ max. Writing 44h does nothing while the resistor is disconnected, and the resistors are disconnected on outputs set to open drain.

All mask bits are 1 at power-up, so no change asserts INT. Clearing a bit to 0 lets that input assert INT. Clearing the mask of an input that has already changed asserts INT at once; setting the mask of the input currently causing an interrupt releases INT.
Read-only. A 1 marks the input that caused the interrupt. The bit of a masked input always reads 0.

Bit 0 (ODEN) sets the whole port: 0 for push-pull, with both the high-side and low-side transistors active, or 1 for open drain, with only the low-side transistor active. Program it before writing 03h to make the pins outputs.

As an input both output transistors are off and the pin is high impedance; it may be taken up to 5.5 V even above VDD(P). As an output the pin is driven low to VSS or high to VDD(P) through low-impedance paths, and the applied voltage should stay within the recommended levels. Each pin has ESD diodes, and all registers return to defaults on power-up or reset.

Applying VDD(P) from 0 V holds the part in reset until VDD(P) reaches VPOR; then the registers and the bus state machine start at their defaults. A later power reset needs VDD(P) taken below VPOR (below 0.2 V for a full cycle) and brought back. The supply ramp rates, re-ramp delay, tolerable glitch depth and width, and the rising and falling trip points are in the supply sequencing table. How a glitch acts on the reset depends on the decoupling, the impedance of the source and that of the device.

Holding RESET LOW for at least tw(rst) puts the registers and the bus state machine in their default state without removing power. Once RESET is HIGH again the port can change. With no active driver, RESET needs a pull-up to VDD(I2C-bus).

Any rising or falling edge on a pin set as input asserts INT after tv(INT). INT releases when the pin returns to its earlier state or when the port that caused it is read; the release happens at the ACK or NACK bit after the rising SCL edge, so a change during that clock pulse may be lost or give only a short pulse. Outputs never cause an interrupt, but turning an output into an input can give a false interrupt if the pin level differs from the input register. INT is open drain and needs a pull-up to VDD(P) or VDD(I2C-bus), to the supply of whatever reads it. With latching on, only a read of the port releases INT.

The master sends the address with R/W = 0, then the command byte, then data. Any number of data bytes may follow in one transfer. Data written to the output port appears on the pins tv(Q) after the acknowledge.

The master writes the address and command byte, sends a repeated START and the address with R/W = 1, then reads data from the chosen register. Any number of bytes may be read; the master leaves the last byte unacknowledged. With the command byte already set to 00h, the master can read the input port directly after the address, and the port data are captured on the ACK clock pulse. A STOP may end the transfer at any time; INT clears on the read and needs no STOP.
SDA and SCL each need a pull-up resistor to a positive supply. SCL and SDA have Schmitt-trigger inputs and a noise filter that rejects spikes up to 50 ns.

Port outputs sink up to 25 mA, enough to drive an LED directly. An off LED tied from VDD to a pin leaves the pin about 1.2 V below VDD, which raises IDD (see ΔIDD). Two ways keep the pin at or above VDD: a high-value resistor across the LED, or running VDD(P) at least 1.2 V below the LED supply.

An enabled pull-up on a pin held LOW draws current from VDD(P) to ground and shows up in IDD. A pull-down on a pin driven HIGH carries current into VSS that IDD does not show; it counts towards the 200 mA VSS limit. The current is linear in voltage and adds pin by pin.
If the centre pad is soldered, connect it only as a second VSS; otherwise leave it open.
